author: Elnaito
quote:
GTA VI: 13 Years, $100, and a Bug Compilation Rockstar Calls a Masterpiece.

We crucified Cyberpunk 2077 for way less than what this thing shipped with. $100 for an incomplete, boring, bugged game. Just a scam, textbook example. 

Start with launch day. Thirteen years of development, and within hours people were falling through the map, clipping through walls, watching planes phase through buildings and NPCs swim sideways like broken animatronics. Crashes in the prologue. The PROLOGUE. On base PS5 and Series X. Softlocks in early Lucia missions. Lost saves. Missing textures. Audio dropping out. PSN buckling under the launch. There's an entire Reddit megathread just to catalogue the damage. "Not even 15 minutes in and a game-breaking bug" isn't a meme, it's a user review.

And it all runs at 30fps. In 2026. On a console exclusive that skipped PC at launch. Driving, the thing you do most in a game literally called Grand Theft AUTO, feels like wading through syrup.

Speaking of the title: Grand Theft Auto, where you can't just grand-theft an auto anymore. Old beaters, sure. Anything modern? Scan it with a phone app, grind a hacking skill, wait for the story to hand you a Key Cloner. Luxury cars come with GPS trackers that ping the cops. Realistic? Congrats. Fun? The one fantasy this franchise is named after is now locked behind a progression system. Hop in, hit the gas, nothing happens. Peak 2026.

That's the real disease: Rockstar confused realism with quality. People watching others play are comparing it to The Sims, not GTA. "You can't just wreak havoc like in GTA 5" is the most damning sentence anyone has said about this game. The world is gorgeous, but every system is built to make chaos cost more and feel worse. Rockstar even admitted they prototyped full grocery runs and fridge restocking. That's where the design head was at. They cut that one feature, but the mindset survived everywhere else: errands, chores, friction, "immersion." Nobody buys a GTA to roleplay a supermarket receipt.

Then the missions. The same railroaded, hand-holding Rockstar formula people have been complaining about since RDR2: follow the marker, stay on the path, take a different route and get "Mission Failed." Thirteen years and the design philosophy is still "watch the cutscene, then do exactly what we tell you."

Now the money. $80 for Standard, $100 for Ultimate. It's the first $80 PS5 game, and it just set the price floor for the whole industry. For that you get single-player only, no online mode, reports of content gated behind the $100 tier, and a "physical edition" that's literally a download code in a box. You pay premium-plus and you don't even get a disc.

And yet: Metacritic 99. Tied with Ocarina of Time. 150+ reviews, almost all perfect, many quietly admitting problems with combat, mission design, performance and bugs, then giving it a 10 anyway. Critics played pre-release builds and barely mentioned what players hit on day one. When a 10/10 sits right next to a bug megathread, the score stops measuring the game and starts measuring access.

Remember Cyberpunk? Pulled from the PlayStation Store, mass refunds, years of apology patches. CD Projekt got dragged through the mud, and rightfully so. GTA VI ships glitchy, at 30fps, gated, overpriced, and it gets a parade. Same crime, different defendant, and this jury showed up with VIP passes.

Will Rockstar patch it? Probably. They have the money and the track record. But "they'll fix it later" was never an excuse for CDPR, and it shouldn't be one for the richest studio in gaming. Thirteen years. $100. This is what they shipped.

author: Elnaito
quote: Bungie's Masterclass in How to Assault Your Eyes, Drain Your Wallet, and Insult Your IntelligenceThe first time I booted up Marathon, the opening cinematic hit me with a strobing, flickering blast of harsh colors and high-contrast chaos. Within thirty minutes, I felt genuinely sick. Not figuratively. I mean the kind of nausea that builds behind your eyes and forces you to look away from the screen. I had to sit in dim light for ten minutes before I could even try the menus. That was my introduction. It did not improve.A UI Designed Without Usability in MindThe user interface is not just bad, it feels aggressively overdesigned. The community calls it "fontslop," and the name fits. Single menu pages stack countless font styles, clashing sizes, ALL CAPS next to regular caps, all fighting for attention against a loud, high-contrast background. There is no visual hierarchy, no clarity, no breathing room.Even major streamers have admitted they cannot tell where they are or what they are looking at. If experienced players are lost, what hope does anyone else have?Inventory items look nearly identical. You end up reading tooltips mid-combat because the icons communicate nothing. Swapping attachments is clunky and wastes space. When players asked for a simpler design, the UI designer publicly embraced the "fontslop merchant" label and said Bungie would never remove the "SAUCE" from the UI. Dismissing usability concerns like that only made things worse.A Visual Style That Feels UnsafeThis goes beyond taste. Marathon’s visual presentation can be physically uncomfortable. The game leans heavily on strobing effects, flicker, and aggressive color cycling. Accessibility guidelines exist to limit flashing visuals that can trigger photosensitive reactions, yet Marathon pushes those boundaries.Players have reported migraines from the opening cinematic and sensory overload from simply navigating menus. Forums are full of people calling it painful to look at. A game that makes players feel ill is not bold art direction, it is a design failure.I had to stop playing more than once because of nausea. Not because it was hard. Because looking at it was exhausting.Monetization Built to FrustrateRunner skins cost 1,120 LUX. The cheapest bundle gives you 1,100 LUX for $10. Always just short. To buy one skin, you effectively spend $15. That gap is not accidental. Currency bundles that leave players slightly under what they need are a well-known psychological **** season "reward pass" offers no meaningful currency returns and resets progression each season. Your gear, upgrades, and grind disappear. You keep cosmetics, nothing more. Bungie calls it a fresh start. In practice, it makes your time feel disposable.A Game Buried Under Its Own FrictionAt its core, there may be potential. The gunplay carries Bungie’s signature feel, and the extraction format could work. But the onboarding is punishing. You start with minimal ammo, supplies are scarce, and death wipes everything you brought in. Hardcore games can demand a lot, but they must first earn trust. Marathon throws players into the deep end without that **** Bigger PictureThis game arrived after layoffs, leadership changes, creative departures, and public controversy. In that context, the final product feels even more disappointing. Players expected a worthy successor to Marathon’s legacy. Instead they received a game that overwhelms the senses, charges premium prices for cosmetics, resets progress, and responds defensively to criticism.Final Verdict: Marathon feels hostile in every direction, visually exhausting, structurally punishing, and aggressively monetized. Its interface is cluttered, its presentation overwhelming, and its seasonal model dismissive of player investment. Some games earn a low score for being dull. This earns it for actively making the experience worse the longer you engage with it.
